yes_case.case: The closest past episodes are the rollout of the Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of (Hybrid &) Electric Vehicles (FAME I in 2015 and FAME II in 2019), as well as the approval of the PM-eBus Sewa scheme in 2023. This current e-bus and e-truck financing scheme differs fundamentally from FAME I and II because those prior iterations primarily focused on upfront demand aggregation and direct purchase subsidies for consumer-facing electric vehicles and general public transport fleets without targeted capital-relief mechanisms like specialized interest subsidies and dedicated credit guarantees for heavy commercial vehicle manufacturers. Furthermore, unlike the PM-eBus Sewa scheme—which relied heavily on a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) bus-operator payment security mechanism managed through state-level urban development frameworks—the upcoming Ministry of Heavy Industries scheme is distinguished by its centralized financial architecture specifically engineered to de-risk heavy commercial vehicle manufacturing and commercial lending at the national level. Despite these structural differences, the recurring policy trajectory shows that whenever the Ministry identifies a severe capital bottleneck in heavy commercial electrification, it moves decisively via formal notifications to deploy targeted fiscal interventions, making the finalization of this scheme an inevitable continuation of past precedent.

no_case.case: The closest past episodes are the rollout of the FAME-II (Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles) scheme modifications in mid-2023 and the transition design phases of the Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme (EMPS) in early 2024. This current e-bus and e-truck financing scheme differs fundamentally from those past episodes in its inclusion of complex credit guarantee structures and interest subsidies targeted directly at commercial heavy-duty manufacturing and asset financing, rather than the straightforward capital subsidies for consumer-facing or light commercial vehicle acquisition used previously. While FAME-II relied on direct upfront purchase incentives disbursed through original equipment manufacturers, a dedicated financing and credit guarantee scheme for heavy e-trucks requires multi-agency alignment involving the Ministry of Finance, public sector banks, and the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust, introducing structural complexities and inter-ministerial friction points absent in the simpler subsidy-disbursement architectures of FAME and EMPS.
